query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dynamic mechanical behavior of as‐solidified, Co‐free equiatomic FeNiCrMn is governed by a transition in deformation mode from uniform dislocation slip at moderate strain rates and ambient temperatures to localized deformation through adiabatic shear band formation at higher strain rates and/or deviating temperatures. In this view, dislocation interactions dominate the strain-hardening behavior under moderate conditions, while at elevated strain rates or altered thermal conditions, local heating and rapid dislocation accumulation trigger shear localization that softens the response.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐solidified, equiatomic FeNiCrMn produced via conventional solidification methods that preserve a balanced microstructure responsible for the alloy’s inherent strength–ductility.
generation.intervention: Perform systematic dynamic mechanical tests (tensile or compressive) with controlled variation in strain rate (from quasi‐static to high dynamic rates) and temperature (sub‐ambient to elevated) combined with microstructural characterization and dislocation dynamics simulations.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under controlled laboratory settings where the as‐solidified microstructure is maintained (i.e., no additional annealing), varying strain rates and temperatures to capture both moderate and extreme deformation regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolving dislocation density and distribution, alongside the formation and propagation of localized adiabatic shear bands.
generation.mechanism: At moderate strain rates and ambient temperatures, uniform dislocation slip and interactions provide strain hardening. In contrast, at higher strain rates or non-ambient temperatures, rapid local deformation leads to localized heating that accelerates dislocation motion, triggers dynamic recrystallization, and ultimately forms adiabatic shear bands, thereby altering the apparent strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A shift in mechanical behavior should be observed: uniform strain hardening and ductile performance at moderate conditions, transitioning to signs of localized deformation (e.g., shear band formation, sudden drops in load or ductility) at higher strain rates or under thermal conditions that promote fast local heating.
generation.baseline: Dynamic tests at quasi-static strain rates (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) and room temperature where the deformation mechanism is expected to be dominated by homogeneous dislocation slip.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to the as‐solidified, Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy retaining its original strength–ductility balance and may not hold if significant microstructural changes (e.g., phase transformation or annealing) occur.
generation.uncertainty: The precise strain rate and temperature thresholds for the transition between deformation modes are not well defined and require iterative refinement through combined experimental and simulation studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of dynamic mechanical tests on as‐solidified FeNiCrMn samples over a matrix of strain rates (from quasi‐static to high dynamic loading) and temperatures (from below ambient to elevated). Combine these tests with high-resolution post-mortem microstructural analysis (TEM and SEM) and local temperature measurements. Complement experiments with dislocation dynamics simulations to map transitions in deformation mechanisms.
measurements: Stress–strain curves under varying strain rates and temperatures
Local temperature measurements (e.g., via infrared thermography)
Microstructural analysis to quantify dislocation density and detect shear bands
Observation of any changes in strain-hardening behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no marked transition from uniform dislocation slip to localized adiabatic shear band formation is observed—in other words, if the mechanical response (stress–strain behavior, strain hardening, and failure mode) remains uniform across all tested strain rates and temperatures without evidence of localized softening or shear bands—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractCompared with traditional alloys, high-entropy alloys have better mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. However, their mechanical properties and microstructural evolution behavior are unclear due to their complex composition. Machine learning has powerful data processing and analysis capabilities, that provides technical advantages for in-depth study of the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys. Thus, we combined machine learning and molecular dynamics to predict the mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloys. The optimal multiple linear regression machine learning algorithm predicts that the optimal composition is Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy, with a tensile strength of 28.25 GPa. Furthermore, molecular dynamics is used to verify the predicted mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys, and it is found that the error between the tensile strength predicted by machine learning and the tensile strength obtained by molecular dynamics simulation is within 0.5%. Moreover, the tensile-compression asymmetry of Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy increased with the increase of temperature and Cu content and the decrease of Fe content.

Equiatomic CoCrNi medium-entropy alloys exhibit superior strength and ductility. In this work, a non-equiatomic CoCrNi alloy with low stacking fault energy was designed, and different fractions of V were added to control the stacking fault energy and lattice distortion. Mechanical properties were evaluated by tensile tests, and deformation microstructures were characterized by transmission electron microscope (TEM). The main deformation mechanisms of CoCrNiV alloy with low V content are dislocation slip, stacking faults, and deformation-induced HCP phase transformation, while the dominant deformation patterns of CoCrNiV alloy with high V contents are dislocation slip and stacking faults. The yield strength increases dramatically when the V content is high, and the strain-hardening behavior changes non-monotonically with increasing the V content. V addition increases the stacking fault energy (SFE) and lattice distortion. The lower strain-hardening rate of 6V alloy than that of 2V alloy is dominated by the SFE. The main conclusions can be summarized as follows:Singe-phase FCC CoCrNiV alloys with different V additions were obtained after solid solution treatment.The plastic deformation of 2V alloy is dominated by dislocation slip, SFs, and HCP martensitic transformation. With increasing the V content, the SFE of CoCrNiV alloy increases, and dislocation slip and SFs prevail in 6V and 10V alloys.The strain-hardening behavior changes non-monotonically with increasing the V content. The lower strain-hardening rate of 6V alloy than that of 2V alloy is dominated by the SFE. The higher strain-hardening rate of 10V alloy than that of 6V alloy is dominated by the lattice distortion.
